To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the self-assembly of meso-monoester of phosphonic acid porphyrin in the presence of metal ions leads to the formation of a dimer, in which the metal ion is bound to the phosphonate group and to the porphyrin nitrogen.
the synthesis of the first example of a self-assembling porphyrin dimer formed by the self-assembly of meso-mono(phosphoryl) porphyrin is presented.

a) the synthesis of a new series of meso-phosphonylated porphyrins bearing peripheral substituents of different nature has been accomplished; b) the synthesis of the corresponding phosphonic acids, which are very unstable in the free form, has been achieved; c) the first example of a self-assembling dimer of porphyrin derivatives has been obtained.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and characterization of new gallium(III), indium(III), and zinc(II) meso-monomonophosphorylporphyrins.

the synthesis and structural characterization of a series of meso-monophosphorylated porphyrins and their metallo complexes with gallium(III), indium(III), and zinc(II) as well as with the synthesis and characterization of the corresponding phosphonic acids and monoesters.
the preparation, characterization and structural analysis of a series of new gallium and indium meso-phosphorylated porphyrins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of the phosphonic acid moiety, which can act as a bidentate ligand, is a crucial factor in determining the self-assembly of these complexes.

in the solid state the self-assembly process is strongly dependent on the peripheral substituents and that it is possible to obtain both dimers (in the case of 5,10,15-tris(p-tolyl)-20-(dioxoethoxyphosphonyl)porphine) and monomeric species [in the case of both 5,10-bis(4-pyridyl)-15,20-bis(p-tol)-porphine and
the self-assembly of the monophosphorylporphyrins in solution and in the solid-state is strongly dependent upon the peripheral substituents of the macrocycles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the coordination of a phosphonate moiety to gallium(III), which is a soft Lewis acid, can be used to control the self-assembly of porphyrins in solution and in the solid-state.

the self-assembled dimers are formed by the self-assembly of the meso-mono(phosphoryl) porphyrin ligands and the metal cations, and the dimerization is controlled by the metal ion and the substituents on the porphyrin ring.

the presence of a meso-monoester substituent on a metal-free tetraarylporphyrin is sufficient to induce the self-assembly of a dimer in the solid state, while the presence of the metal ion prevents the formation of the self-assembly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the self-assembly process can be controlled by the nature of the metal cation and the peripheral substituents on the porphyrin ring.
the coordination of the metal cation with the phosphonate group of the meso-substituent of the porphyrin ring is a key factor for the formation of self-assembled dimers.

the coordination of a gallium(III)/indium(III) ion by the phosphorus atom of the meso-phosphoryl group of a porphyrin molecule is not sufficient to induce the formation of the corresponding dimers, and that a further coordination of the oxygen atom of this group is required.
